paragraphs.title: A Cry from Distress and Restlessness

easy.explanation: The psalm begins, “I cried unto God with my voice.”
easy.q: Unto whom does the speaker cry?

easy.explanation: He says, “In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord.”
easy.q: What does the speaker seek in the day of trouble?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “my soul refused to be comforted.”
easy.q: What does the speaker’s soul refuse to do?

answers: His distress continued through the night
medium.explanation: The phrase describes continuing distress and restlessness at night.
medium.q: What is meant by the statement that the speaker’s sore “ran in the night”?
How does the speaker describe his spirit?

answers: He causes the speaker to sleep
medium.explanation: The first verse says, “and he gave ear unto me.”
medium.q: What does God do when the speaker cries unto Him?

answers: He is too troubled to speak
challenge.explanation: He says, “I am so troubled that I cannot speak.”
challenge.q: What does the speaker’s inability to speak reveal about his condition?

answers: Crying, distress, troubled thoughts, and speechlessness
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from crying to trouble, an overwhelmed spirit, sleeplessness, and silence.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the speaker’s experience?

answers: The speaker’s persistent cry for divine attention
The speaker’s interest in the weather
challenge.explanation: Repeating his cry to God emphasizes the intensity and persistence of his distress.
challenge.q: What does the repeated appeal to God emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Remembering the Past and Questioning Divine Kindness

easy.explanation: He says, “I have considered the days of old.”
He says, “I call to remembrance my song in the night.”
easy.q: What does he remember in the night?

answers: Whether it is gone for ever
Whether it will lead an army
Whether it is found in the sea
easy.explanation: He asks, “Is his mercy clean gone for ever?”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask about God’s mercy?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “I commune with mine own heart.”
medium.q: What does the speaker do with his own heart?

answers: From remembering the past to questioning God’s present favor
From describing the sea to describing thunder
From celebrating victory to appointing a leader
medium.explanation: Memory leads the speaker to ask whether God’s favor, mercy, and compassion have ended.
medium.q: What is the main movement in this passage?

medium.explanation: In context, “favourable” refers to God showing kindness and acceptance.
medium.q: In the question “will he be favourable no more?”, what does “favourable” mean?

answers: His memories lead to painful questions about God’s mercy
He is occupied with leading a flock
challenge.explanation: His remembrance is followed by questions about whether God has cast off His people and withheld mercy.
challenge.q: Why does remembering the past not immediately comfort the speaker?

answers: Ancient days are remembered while present distress raises difficult questions
Dry land is contrasted with the sea
challenge.explanation: The speaker looks back to ancient times but struggles with questions about his present situation.
challenge.q: What contrast appears in the passage?

answers: Distress and uncertainty about continued mercy
Complete confidence that every problem is solved
A desire to describe nature only
challenge.explanation: The questions about casting off, mercy, grace, and compassion reveal the speaker’s anguish and uncertainty.
challenge.q: What do the many questions about God express?

easy.explanation: He says, “I will remember the works of the LORD.”
easy.q: What does the speaker determine to remember?

answers: A God who rules the sea alone
easy.explanation: The speaker declares, “Thou art the God that doest wonders.”
easy.q: What kind of God is described in these verses?

answers: The sons of Jacob and Joseph
easy.explanation: The verse says God redeemed “the sons of Jacob and Joseph.”

answers: He meditates on them and talks of them
He refuses to speak about them
medium.explanation: He says, “I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings.”
medium.q: What does the speaker do with God’s works?

answers: Who is so great a God as our God?
Where is the path through the sea?
medium.explanation: The speaker connects God’s holy way with the question of His incomparable greatness.
medium.q: What question follows the statement that God’s way is in the sanctuary?

medium.explanation: Here, “wonders” refers to extraordinary acts performed by God.
medium.q: In the phrase “doest wonders,” what does “wonders” mean?

answers: He turns from troubling questions to remembering God’s deeds
He turns from remembrance to sleep
He turns from hope to believing God does nothing
challenge.explanation: Instead of dwelling only on whether mercy has ended, he deliberately remembers God’s works and wonders.
challenge.q: What change occurs in the speaker’s outlook?

answers: God acted powerfully for His people
challenge.explanation: God redeemed His people “with thine arm,” emphasizing His active and powerful deliverance.
challenge.q: What does the mention of redemption emphasize?

answers: Remembering works, meditating on wonders, recognizing God’s greatness, and recalling redemption
challenge.explanation: The speaker remembers God’s works, reflects on them, praises His greatness, and recalls His redemption of His people.
challenge.q: Which sequence best summarizes the passage?

paragraphs.title: Divine Manifestation in the Sea and Guidance of the People

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The waters saw thee, O God.”
easy.q: What saw God, according to the passage?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions clouds, thunder, lightning, and the trembling earth.

answers: Like a flock by Moses and Aaron
Like an army by a king
easy.explanation: The final verse says, “Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.”
easy.q: How did God lead His people?

answers: Thunder, lightning, and the waters display His power
The storm prevents God from acting
The storm describes the speaker’s sleep
medium.explanation: The powerful natural imagery portrays the majesty and power of God’s manifestation.
medium.q: How does the storm imagery reveal God’s presence?

answers: God makes a way through the waters
The sea prevents the people from moving
medium.explanation: The verse presents the sea as a place where God’s path and power are revealed.
medium.q: What does “Thy way is in the sea” suggest?

answers: The deep parts of the waters
medium.explanation: “The depths” refers to the deep waters that were troubled.
medium.q: In the phrase “the depths,” what is being described?

answers: God’s work is evident, but His precise ways remain mysterious
There was no path through the sea
Moses and Aaron did not lead the people
challenge.explanation: God’s path is seen in His mighty acts, but His footsteps cannot be fully traced or understood.
challenge.q: What does “thy footsteps are not known” suggest?

answers: It recalls that God can make a way and lead His people
It proves that the people were left without guidance
It describes only fear of the storm
challenge.explanation: God’s path through the sea and His guidance of the people show His power to deliver and lead.
challenge.q: How can the sea imagery inspire hope?

answers: From the power of nature to the ordered guidance of the people
From questioning mercy to forgetting God
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from waters, thunder, lightning, and trembling earth to God leading His people like a flock.
challenge.q: What transition occurs in these verses?
